questions.prompt: You are applying Understanding the Cyber Threat Landscape to a new scenario. What is the best first step?
options: Define scope and expected behavior, collect relevant evidence, and verify the result in an authorized or synthetic environment.
Repeat the same test against unrelated public systems to collect more data.
Disable useful logging so the test output looks simpler.
Assume an unfamiliar result proves malicious intent without corroboration.
questions.answer_key: Define scope and expected behavior, collect relevant evidence, and verify the result in an authorized or synthetic environment.
questions.explanation: Bound the work, define expected behavior, and collect relevant evidence in a safe and authorized context before drawing conclusions.

questions.prompt: Which statement best summarizes the main idea of The Cyberattack Lifecycle?
options: The Cyberattack Lifecycle focuses on reconnaissance concepts; initial access; execution and persistence. Define the system or data in scope, the expected behavior, and the consequences if that behavior fails. Then select a proportionate control and identify evidence that can verify both the normal path and an important failure case.
A single successful test proves that a system is completely secure in every environment.
The fastest workflow is always to skip evidence collection and make changes directly in production.
Security responsibilities disappear when a technical tool has been installed.
questions.answer_key: The Cyberattack Lifecycle focuses on reconnaissance concepts; initial access; execution and persistence. Define the system or data in scope, the expected behavior, and the consequences if that behavior fails. Then select a proportionate control and identify evidence that can verify both the normal path and an important failure case.
questions.explanation: The lesson's core idea is: The Cyberattack Lifecycle focuses on reconnaissance concepts; initial access; execution and persistence. Define the system or data in scope, the expected behavior, and the consequences if that behavior fails. Then select a proportionate control and identify evidence that can verify both the normal path and an important failure case. The other options overstate what one test or tool can prove and ignore the need for context, evidence, and governance.
